en: The warriors enjoying themselves—
All forty made ready together.
Into Khan Manas's presence,
They entered in a crowd.
“God knows whether in Talas
You will come and alight again,
Whether after this, from my hands,
You will return and eat again.”
Relating her spoken words,
She brought them into the court,
With Khan Manas at their head.
Entertaining the forty warriors,
A dining cloth woven of silk,
Your sister-in-law now brought and spread.
In Kanykey's heart
Was the longing to host them.
Upon golden and silver platters,
She had six mares slaughtered.
Rib fat, thick intestine, neck fat and tail,
She had meat cut up and ready.
At that time, the forty warriors
Of Kanykey, Karakan's daughter,
Now saw the nobility.
Spirits, wine and fermented mare's milk,
She set among them now.
Champion Manas and the forty warriors,
Drinking spirits, growing breathless,
Drinking fermented mare's milk, belching fat,
After they had finished eating,
Had the dining cloth cleared away
And gave a resounding blessing.
To mount their horses,
They now rose in a thunderous bustle.
Khan Manas mounted and set out,
His forty warriors beside him,
“I shall campaign against Beijing,” he said,
At fifty-two years of age.
His forefather was Tümön Khan;
From Tümön Khan came Böyön Khan;
From Böyön Khan came Chayan Khan;
From Chayan Khan came Karakan;
From Karakan came Khan Jakyp.
From Khan Jakyp came young Manas,
Who fired shots at eleven.
When he reached twelve,
He broke courts and raided peoples.
When he reached fifteen years,
He became leader of a people with a court.
When he reached sixteen,
Not even twelve realms challenged him.
At that time, before Manas,
No one remained to oppose him.
“Toward fortified Beijing,
I shall face it and thrust my spear,” he said.
“From the still, vast hell,
I shall set my soul free,” he said.
“At the looming Chinese,
I shall aim and thrust my spear,” he said.
“From hell with its grievous suffering,
I shall set my soul free,” he said.
“The decree Allah has imposed,
If it falls on my neck, I shall face it,” he said.
“If my appointed death comes in Beijing,
I shall die exchanging fire,” he said.
“To fortified Beijing,
My heart is set; I shall go,” he said.
“Beijing's khan, Kongurbay,
I shall face him and wage war,” he said.
“If my plans succeed, in Beijing,
Almambet and Chubak,
The daring one born a lion,
I shall make them governors and return,” he said.
“The seething Chinese people's
Great herds I shall scatter,” he said.
“I shall open their treasury,” he said.
Ajybay, Bakay, hero Chubak,
Lion Syrgak, born a lion,
Their spear-points swaying,
The forty wolves followed behind him.
Their swords ringing,
Pied banners and painted spears,
Outstanding champions the world could not defeat,
Who thrust their spears and did not withdraw,
Who did not flee the enemy in fear,
Who fastened their belts across their waists—
If an enemy aimed weapons at them,
Each one attacked a thousand.
In Afghanistan and India,
Manas had long ago raised dust.
The great peoples of right and left
Marveled at Manas's might.
Battle-axes flashing at their waists,
The forty warriors born as lions
Went away with a clatter.
Noble-born Khan Manas
Went majestically at the front.
Crying like a white goshawk,
His Akkelte flashing,
The lion noble Khan Manas
Cried out like a white falcon.
Akkula beneath him,
A hardy crossbred horse, a famed racer,
With sieve-like lungs and copper forelegs—
Ridden for six months, he would not tire.
Until his sixtieth year of maturity,
His fangs would not wear down with age.
No moon-hoofed horse on earth
Could equal Akkula.
His Akkula beneath him,
His forty warriors beside him,
He had circled the Altay mountains,
Devastated peoples far away,
And readied every item of equipment.
He had wound round the Ural mountains.
Through the champion's ancestral spirit,
Akkula, the surpassingly swift,
Turned his neck like a stag.
If a ravine an arrow-shot wide appeared,
He ran on without delay.
Hearing that he was a wondrous steed,
Knowing that he was a tireless racer,
Offering gold and precious metal by weight,
The khan of Bukhara asked for him.
Far from giving Kula away,
No one without ritual washing had ridden him.
His soles hammered upon the earth;
The bit forged of gold
Clattered within his throat.
His back curved like a round pot-stand.
In the night, the damned creature
Ran and sprang like an ibex,
Clashing his bit,
His tail like strands of silk
Lashing against his thighs,
Striding forward with a lunge,
Jerking like a saker falcon,
His four legs like ravines,
His hollowed front teeth
Like steel beaten into shape.
Flattening his ears, making them short,
Letting no mortal approach his side,
Glancing sideways and looking back,
His behavior unlike other horses',
His gait different, striding wide,
No wind matching his trot,
No shot matching his gallop,
When a ringing “Go!” was cried,
The sound could not catch him at once.
With leopard Manas at their head,
Turning toward Beijing,
The red banner with its golden crescent
Raised and carried before them,
All the forty warriors,
Behind Khan Manas,
Went away in high spirits.
What all of them wore
Were matching helmets forged of iron.
There was no gap over their whole bodies;
All were uniformly dark blue.
All the forty warriors
Would not submit their will to anyone.
Among mortals upon the earth,
No one remained to oppose them.
They packed their ammunition pouches with shot.
If enemies stood to right or left,
Hearing their fame, those enemies fled in fear.
They dwelt and pastured in Keng-Kol;
Their wondrous steeds, with proper care,
They kept tethered for war.
If an enemy bore a grudge,
His misery began before a shot was fired.
Setting grassy ground ablaze,
They poured blood into dark water.
Hardened by drinking blood,
Named leopard warriors,
They trained their steeds and made them prance,
Made the enemies they met crawl.
They did not turn their faces away in gloom.
If a host came shouting battle cries,
The forty warriors, each worth a thousand,
Did not stand watching in fear.
Who spears the enemy, if he is speared?
The lion warriors alone spear him;
The name and fame remain with Manas.
When Manas became Manas,
When the forty warriors camped beside Manas,
When all the warriors came,
They made his yurt-felts rich with fat.
Slaughtering Manas's enemies,
They made every side of him run with blood.
They made his lattice walls rich with fat.
Hearing Manas's wrath,
They made his fame fill the whole world.
If an enemy spurred forward,
Slaughtering and destroying, the forty warriors
Filled heaven and earth with dust.
If an enemy taking aim appeared,
They leveled him with the black earth.
His forty warriors beside him,
Your wolf-maned Manas, favored by Kydyr,
Caught up with the vast host.
A man endowed with sacred powers,
Golden forelock and tasselled belt,
Azizkan's only son,
To put the host in order,
To take the count of the host,
Champion Almambet had become khan.
Almambet, the son of a khan,
Did not abandon the marks of khanship;
He would not lead a disorderly host.
Of Black Chinese Beijing,
Almambet had seen the army.
Dug around its edge,
Almambet had seen the moat.
Kongurbay, the unbelievers'
Lion, Almambet had seen.
Whose number no mortal knew,
Almambet had seen the people.
All of Esenkan's
Warriors, Almambet had seen.
He had been a solidly built fortress.
In majestic Beijing,
Almambet, Azizkan's son,
Had been khan for twenty-one years.
Every skill of the Chinese,
Had he not come knowing it?
The firmly founded city of Beijing,
Had he not left it and come?
Wreaking havoc upon Beijing,
Had he not taken the lead and come?
Letting his mother pass as a martyr,
Had he not given her up and come?
The fiendish nature of the Chinese,
Had he not seen it before coming?
“When making a journey to Beijing,
If one does not count the host,
It will bring disaster,” he thought.
“Unless we go to Beijing in this way,
When the many Chinese meet us,
They will slaughter us all,” he thought.
The lion had no other course;
His eyes flashed as he looked about.
The Muslims' red banner,
To Koshoy, elder of the people,
He brought and put it in his hands.
His courage was no less;
Though Koshoy had grown old,
He was no hero the people could belittle.
A prince from the beginning,
Called “Khan Koshoy,”
Who dwelt in broad Alay,
Who ranged along broad Kashgar,
When enemies came in his time,
He flashed like a flint.
Wearing a coat like blue iron,
Riding a horse like Chalkuyruk,
